translationRepairs: He did not praise Wu's burial rites like Qin Zheng, ridicule stone coffins while praising thick firewood.
He condemned Qin Zheng and praised the burial rites of Wu, scoffing at stone outer coffins and admiring thick firewood.
非秦政而褒吳禮 contrasts condemning Qin Zheng with praising the burial rites of Wu; the old English reverses and muddles that contrast.
He did not praise Wu's burial rites like the First Emperor of Qin, ridicule stone coffins while praising thick firewood.
He condemned the First Emperor of Qin's extravagance and praised the frugal burial rites of Wu, scoffing at stone vaults and admiring the ancient practice of covering the dead with thick firewood.
The memorial praises frugal burial: 非秦政 contrasts the First Emperor's extravagance with the rites of Wu, while 厚薪 evokes the ancient practice of covering the dead with firewood.
Duke Hui of Shao Hao was the Grand Progenitor's eldest elder brother.
Hao, Duke Hui of Shao, was the Grand Progenitor's eldest brother.
The proposal removes the duplicated adjective, but placing Hao after Shao still makes it look like part of the territorial title. This wording separates the personal name from the title.
Yuwen Hui, style name Ganren loved learning from childhood and was clever and bright.
Yuwen Hui, courtesy name Ganren, loved learning from childhood and was intelligent.
字 introduces a courtesy name. The revision fixes the missing punctuation and uses natural English for 聰惠.
When the Grand Progenitor had pacified Qin and Long, Shifen was killed by Duke of Qi Shenwu.
When the Grand Progenitor had pacified Qin and Long, Shifen was killed by Emperor Shenwu of Northern Qi.
齊神武 is Gao Huan's retrospective posthumous title, Emperor Shenwu of Northern Qi, and is not a dukedom.
After Grand Progenitor Yuwen Tai had pacified Qin and Long, Shifen was killed by Gao Huan, Duke of Qi Shenwu.
After Grand Progenitor Yuwen Tai had pacified Qin and Long, Shifen was killed by Gao Huan.
The idiomatic field should use Gao Huan's standard personal name and remove the invented title Duke of Qi Shenwu.

Duke of Qi Shenwu crossed the river and invaded Fengyi; the Grand Progenitor led his army into Guan from Hongnong. Dao directed the left and right imperial guard, joined at Shaye, fought Duke of Qi Shenwu, and inflicted a great defeat.

Emperor Shenwu of Northern Qi crossed the river and invaded Fengyi; the Grand Progenitor led his army into Guan from Hongnong. Dao directed the left and right imperial guard, joined at Shayuan, fought Emperor Shenwu of Northern Qi, and inflicted a great defeat.
The proposal correctly renders the retrospective title 齊神武 and corrects the place-name 沙苑 from Shaye to Shayuan.

When Gao Huan, Duke of Qi Shenwu, crossed the river and invaded Fengyi, Grand Progenitor Yuwen Tai led his army into Guan from Hongnong. Yuwen Dao directed the left and right imperial guard, joined at Shaye, fought Gao Huan, and inflicted a great defeat.

When Gao Huan crossed the Yellow River and invaded Fengyi, Grand Progenitor Yuwen Tai led his army into the passes from Hongnong. Yuwen Dao led the imperial guards to join him at Shayuan, where they fought Gao Huan and inflicted a crushing defeat.
The revised English accurately identifies 河 as the Yellow River, 入關 as entering the passes, and 沙苑 as Shayuan while making the battle sequence clear.
Yuan Bao was killed by Qi Shenwu.
Yuanbao was killed by Emperor Shenwu of Northern Qi.
元寶 is the single personal name Yuanbao, and 齊神武 is the retrospective title Emperor Shenwu of Northern Qi.
Yuan Bao was killed by Qi Shenwu.
Yuwen Yuanbao was killed by Gao Huan.
The chapter identifies Yuanbao as a Yuwen clansman, and Gao Huan is the clear standard English name for 齊神武 in idiomatic prose.
His son Puti was killed by Qi Shenwu.
His son Puti was killed by Emperor Shenwu of Northern Qi.
The literal field should render 齊神武 as Emperor Shenwu of Northern Qi rather than treating Qi Shenwu as a personal name.
His son Puti was killed by Qi Shenwu.
His son Puti was killed by Gao Huan.
The idiomatic field should identify the killer by his standard personal name, Gao Huan.
When Duke of Qi Shenwu attacked Shayuan, Xing was among the ranks; the army was defeated and he was taken captive, and by precedent was dispersed and assigned to various armies.

When Emperor Shenwu of Northern Qi attacked Shayuan, Xing was in the ranks; his army was defeated, he was captured, and according to standard practice he was dispersed and assigned to one of the armies.
The proposal correctly renders 齊神武 and makes the captive Xing, rather than the defeated army, the subject of 隨例散配諸軍.
When Gao Huan, Duke of Qi Shenwu, attacked Shayuan, Xing was among the ranks; the army was defeated and he was taken captive, and by precedent was dispersed and assigned to various armies.
When Gao Huan attacked at Shayuan, Yuwen Xing was serving in the ranks. His army was defeated and he was captured; under the usual practice for captives, he was assigned to one of the army units.
The proposal correctly removes the false dukedom and clarifies the subjects. This revision states the captive-assignment sense of 隨例散配諸軍 more directly.

At the end of the Daxiang era (579–581), when Emperor Wen of Sui served as regent, Zhou raised the provincial troops to support Yuchi Jiong; he fought Prince of Qinghe Yang Su, was defeated, fled, was captured at Shiji, and beheaded.

At the end of the Daxiang era (579–581), when Emperor Wen of Sui served as regent, Zhou raised the provincial troops to support Yuchi Jiong and fought Yang Su, Duke of Qinghe. Defeated, he fled, but was caught at Shiji and beheaded.
清河公 is Duke of Qinghe, not Prince. Reordering the English title and separating the clauses also makes Zhou the subject of the defeat, flight, capture, and execution.
Soon afterward he was executed for a capital offense.
Soon afterward he was executed for his association with Prince of Wei Yuwen Zhi.
坐直誅 says Bin was executed on account of Yuwen Zhi. Naming the Prince of Wei distinguishes him from Yuwen Zhi (至), the different man named immediately above.
Soon afterward he was executed for a direct offense.
Soon afterward he was executed on account of Prince of Wei Yuwen Zhi.
直 is the personal name of the Prince of Wei, not the adjective direct. The full name prevents confusion with Yuwen Zhi (至).

字 introduces the courtesy name Yongluo; this is more natural and precise than the bare noun style or the verb styled.
